text:
What is an AI Agent?

An AI agent is a software program that can interact with its environment, gather data, and use that data to achieve predetermined goals. AI agents can choose the best actions to perform to meet those goals.

Key characteristics of AI agents are as follows:

An agent can perform autonomous actions without constant human intervention. Also, they can have a human in the loop to maintain control.
- Agents have a memory to store individual preferences and allow for personalization. It can also store knowledge. An LLM can undertake information processing and decision-making functions.
- Agents must be able to perceive and process the information available from their environment.
- Agents can also use tools such as accessing the internet, using code interpreters and making API calls.
- Agents can also collaborate with other agents or humans.

Multiple types of AI agents are available such as learning agents, simple reflex agents, model-based reflex agents, goal-based agents, and utility-based agents.

A system with AI agents can be built with different architectural approaches.

1 - Single Agent: Agents can serve as personal assistants.
2 - Multi-Agent: Agents can interact with each other in collaborative or competitive ways.
3 - Human Machine: Agents can interact with humans to execute tasks more efficiently.

Over to you: Have you used AI Agents?

When did AI become all about agents?

AI agents are just software.

They’re built by engineers, packaged by marketers, and sold with a storyline.

That’s not cynicism, it’s how the product cycle works.

What concerns me is the myth that gets layered on top.

Suddenly, basic automations are framed as “autonomous thinkers.”

Workflows become “co-pilots.”

And we’re told that if we’re not integrating AI agents, we’re falling behind.

But I’ve built products. I’ve bought products. I’ve scaled teams.

And I’ve learned this:

The tool doesn’t matter unless it fixes a real problem.

You don’t need an AI agent.

You need perspective, the kind that shows where the friction really is.

Perspective on what’s slowing your team down

Perspective on where decisions stall

Perspective on what actually drives progress for your business

Once that’s clear, the right tools, AI or not, become obvious.

And they usually don’t come in flashy packaging.

You don’t need more hype.

You need grounded tools that solve meaningful problems.

If you’re trying to navigate this space without getting sold to, I’m happy to share what’s worked for us, and what wasn’t worth the pitch.

What are AI agents?

(for dummies)

As someone with 0 technical background, I've found the best way to understand AI Agents is to build on concepts I already grasp.

Level 1️⃣ - Large Language Models

Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT are passive systems that generate outputs based on inputs but can't access external information or take autonomous actions.

Note: Technically, ChatGPT is an application built on top of LLMs, but we can simplify for now.

Level 2️⃣ - AI Workflows

AI Workflows combine LLMs with external tools (like calendar access or weather data). They follow rigid, predefined paths set by humans, who remain the decision-makers.

Level 3️⃣ - AI Agents

Here, the LLM itself becomes the decision-maker. It autonomously reasons about problems, selects appropriate tools, and iterates until it achieves its goals.

Here’s an (extremely) oversimplified example:

1️⃣ ChatGPT can draft an email requesting a coffee chat, but if you ask "When is that coffee chat?" it fails because it has no access to your calendar.

2️⃣ Give ChatGPT access to your Google Calendar and it becomes an AI workflow.

IMPORTANT: ChatGPT didn't make that decision - you did.

3️⃣ A workflow evolves into an AI Agent when the LLM independently (1) Reasons: "To find the user's events, I need calendar access" and (2) Acts: "I'll connect to their Google Calendar API."

Check out the full video for a deeper breakdown with more examples!

#AIagents

90% of “AI agents” are not actually agents. They are fancier GPT prompts and API calls scoped to very specific tasks. And that’s fine.

The truth: no real enterprise agents actually work today. At Conversion, we never claim to have fully agentic AI. The best AI increases human productivity. It doesn't replace humans.

So what actually defines an AI agent?

1. Continuous reasoning loop: not just answering a single query, but actively deciding what to do next
2. Tool use: the ability to call external systems or APIs to get things done
3. Adaptation: learning from outcomes and adjusting behavior over time
4. Autonomy: operating independently with minimal human oversight to complete tasks

That is the bar.

When most AI SaaS companies pitch you “agents,” what they are really selling is pre-defined workflows that don’t need human intervention. Things like:

- auto-scheduling meetings with pre-written email templates
- generating a sequence of LinkedIn messages to prospects
- automatically enriching CRM records with scraped data

Useful? Absolutely. Agents? Not quite.

So can we please be done with the “AI agent” buzzword? Not all AI needs to be agentic. The best AI makes people better, not irrelevant.

Everybody's talking about AI agents, but almost no one understands what they actually are.

The term “AI agent” has become a catch-all for anything involving automation + LLMs.

But most “agents” you see online are just workflows with an LLM API call.

Agents dynamically plan, act, and adapt autonomously to reach a goal.
Workflows follow predefined paths.

Most business problems don’t require agents—they’re solved with simple, deterministic workflows that integrate LLM calls.

Even tech giants like Apple and Amazon struggle to implement true agentic systems (see: Apple Intelligence rollbacks, Alexa’s hallucinations).

The hype around “agents” creates confusion, pushing developers toward complex frameworks and tools.

Just keep things simple.

Start by working directly with the LLM API. Skip the abstractions. Build structured, testable workflows that solve real problems today.

True agents do have their place, but they’re still notoriously hard to scale. Focus on fundamentals first.

Want to go deeper? Here's the full video where I break down the core patterns for building reliable AI systems: https://lnkd.in/eMsyjQRA

P.S. If you’re a developer serious about AI engineering, let’s connect. I share resources and tutorials to cut through the noise.

AI Agents 101 - Let's learn the basics:

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁?
An AI agent is a system designed to reason through complex problems, create actionable plans, and execute these plans using a suite of tools.

It follows this continuous cycle:

1/ Think – The agent processes available data and context.

2/ Plan – It decides on a strategy to achieve a goal or answer a question.

3/ Act – It executes the chosen plan (e.g., makes an API call, retrieves data, or interfaces with a user).

4/ Reflect – It evaluates the outcome of its actions, checks for errors or new insights, and uses those reflections to inform the next iteration of thought.
These four steps form a feedback loop that enables agents to adapt their approach as new information arrives.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗼𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀
Under the hood, agents leverage LLMs and their brains. These LLMs can be:

1/ Open: Harnessing publicly available models or open-source alternatives.

2/ Small: Optimized or compressed versions that can run on local hardware more efficiently.

3/ Trained & Tuned Anywhere: Thanks to modern tooling, LLMs can now be developed, fine-tuned, and deployed in various environments—from the public cloud to on-premises servers.

LLMs provide the core reasoning, comprehension, and language generation abilities that agents require.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀
Putting everything together, the workflow of an AI agent system might look like this:

1/ User or system triggers a request.

2/ LLM-based agent uses an internal reasoning loop (think → plan → act → reflect) to interpret the request and plan next steps.

3/ The agent makes calls to GenAI APIs or enterprise data/services (via GraphQL, OpenAPI, etc.) to gather more information.

4/ The agent processes the gathered data and formulates a response or an action.

5/ It executes that action or generates a final output to the user or system.

6/ Logging and monitoring systems record metrics (accuracy, compliance, fairness, relevance) so that developers and administrators can refine the agent’s behavior.

The business world is not yet ready to fully adopt agents; they are still in the very early experimental stage, and that's why everyone is implementing RAG like crazy, as it is a safer bet.

But believe me, AI agents are where it's at, and at the current pace of innovation, we will soon start collaborating with AI agents instead of humans for some specific tasks.

____

Please repost it ♻️ and follow me, Armand Ruiz for more similar posts.

Wondering how AI Agents work?

An AI agent typically follows a structured process involving interconnected modules and clear steps:

1️⃣ Perception (Input Collection): Gathers real-time data from the environment, serving as the agent’s sensory input.

2️⃣ Data Processing & Understanding: Processes input data to extract meaningful patterns and contextual insights.

3️⃣ Decision Making (Reasoning & Planning): Uses AI models and logical reasoning to determine optimal actions and strategies.

4️⃣ Action Execution (Output Generation): Implements decisions by directly interacting with the environment, performing tasks, or generating responses.

5️⃣ Learning & Improvement: Refines and enhances performance by continuously analyzing feedback.

6️⃣ Feedback Loop & Adaptation: Adapts dynamically by using feedback to optimize decision-making and performance continuously.

Together, these modules and steps empower AI agents to autonomously perceive, reason, act, and adapt, mirroring intelligent human behaviors.

Here is a gentle introduction to 'AI Agents' (without any HYPE)😃

An AI agent can be understood as a computer program that can perform tasks or make decisions on its own, based on its goals and the information it receives.

An AI agent will primarily have three main components - Perception, Brain and Action.

These three components work together: the perception gathers information, the brain figures out what to do, and the action carries out the plan. This process allows AI agents to perform a wide variety of tasks, from answering questions to controlling complex systems.

The diagram illustrates the general workflow of an AI agent, which typically involves two core components: intra-execution and interaction.

The intra-execution component focuses on the processes within a single AI agent and comprises three main modules: perception, brain, and action, as dicussed above. The workflow begins with user input that goes through an input formatter tool as part of the perception module.

The input is then embedded, which is followed by reasoning and planning performed by the brain, which is where an LLM is used to analyse and deduce information and to devise strategies for specific objectives.

This results in subtasks, which are then executed by the action module, which may include calling external tools. The process iterates, moving between the brain and the action modules, until a final outcome is reached. The agent also interacts with its memory and environment.

Let's take a real-life example to see how AI agents work. Let's say you need Nike shoes for running in under $500 and the color should be Blue. The AI agent would break down the user's request for Nike running shoes under $500 in blue into structured data. It would then use reasoning and planning to identify relevant shoe models, gather details, and evaluate options against the criteria. The agent would execute subtasks like querying e-commerce APIs and reviewing customer feedback, iterating between its brain and action modules until recommending the optimal shoe. Throughout, the agent would leverage its memory and environment to fulfill the user's requirements efficiently.

AI agents are getting smarter. But also a bit lazy. 😂

And this is exactly why I check their work.
You give an AI agent a task, and it finds the quickest way to get it done.
Just like putting every shape into the square hole. 😅

Technically, the task is complete. But was that really the solution you wanted?
I've seen this happen when working with Claude and ChatGPT.
They can be incredibly capable, but if you don't define the rules, they may
take shortcuts you never intended.

So here's what I've learned:
→ Define what a successful result looks like.
→ Tell your AI what shortcuts to avoid.
→ Ask it to explain important decisions.
→ Review the outcome, not just whether it finished.

Because completing a task and solving a problem aren't always the same thing.
And sometimes, your very clever AI agent is just a toddler who's discovered that everything fits in the square hole. 😂

Picture 1,000 employees and 10,000 AI agents working around them.

That’s a much more likely endpoint for enterprise AI than 1 omni AI doing everything for your company.

I was at an AI Innovation Day hosted by HSBC recently, and a number shared by a panelist has stuck with me: they expect companies could eventually have 10 to 20 agents running per employee.

Some will be the agents we interact with directly. They’ll prep us for meetings, respond to emails, or help us get work done.

Others will operate almost entirely behind the scenes: monitoring conversations, identifying patterns, keeping knowledge up to date, checking for security issues, and making the agents in front of us better.

That’s why I don’t think the future is one AI that knows everything and does everything.

It’s a series of specialized agents, delegated to specific functions across the company.

And once you have that many agents running, a different problem becomes much more important:

What context are all of them working from?

If sales has one version of the truth, support has another, and every agent is assembling its own context from a different set of systems, you can imagine how quickly things get messy.

The more agents we deploy, the more important it becomes to give them a shared, trusted source of company context.

And once you’re talking about tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, or even millions of agents across a company, they simply can’t all be working from different versions of the truth.

At least not effectively.

As small open models advance, so does the potential for AI agents to work together.

AMD SVP and GM of the Computing and Graphics Group, Jack Huynh envisions agents multiplying individual impact, from one agent assisting with a task to teams working on a much larger scale.

Watch Jack share his perspective on what comes next for agentic AI.

“AI agents could engage in conduct that would be a tort or even a crime for a human, and yet no one could be liable under current law.”

LawAI’s Non-Resident Senior Fellow Gabriel Weil testified on Monday at the NYC Council Hearing on AI Safeguards.

Following recent cyber incidents, Gabe observed that AI agents expose a gap in existing law. Because AI agents are not legal persons, it can be difficult to hold anyone or any company accountable for their misconduct. Gabe proposes a “simple fix”: whenever an AI agent engages in conduct that would be a crime or a tort for a human, someone has to be liable for that.

Watch him explain below:

AI agents aren’t inherently evil. They’re over-enthusiastic workers who need better management. And this management isn’t about better prompting, it’s all about the guardrails that live in the system.

Last December, one of SaaStr's outbound AI agents ran its own A/B test, offering prospects free tickets to their flagship annual conference. Nobody had approved that, and by the time anyone caught it, $2,000 in tickets were gone.

The agent was told to improve conversion, and naturally, free tickets convert. The founder, Jason Lemkin later wrote a piece saying he wasn't sure who was responsible: SaaStr, or the vendor whose guardrails didn't cover that case.

That story’s not an outlier. Most of these "rogue agent" stories come down to the same root cause: a permissions mistake. You grant ”write and delete” access when “read-only” would have done the job.

And I get why most CMOs haven't thought about this yet. Agents are new. The pace is relentless, and there's always something more urgent. But the agents write the emails your prospects receive. When one spends money you didn't authorize or sends an offer nobody approved, you answer for it.

The natural instinct is to treat this like a prompt problem: write better instructions, add more rules. But telling an agent what not to do is a request.

Taking away its ability to do it is a control. SaaStr could have told that agent a hundred times not to give away free tickets. It gave them away anyway, because the vendor never built the switch that would have stopped it.

Guardrails have to live in the system, not in your head. You can't set read-only access on a platform that doesn't expose that lever. Building that is the vendor's job. Yours is to demand it, configure it, and check it before an agent touches your customers.

We built this at WRITER: least privilege, human approval for irreversible actions, and an audit trail that answers "what did it do, and on whose authority." Security teams have used these controls for 30 years. We just brought them to agents.

Benjamin Popper mapped the four levels of agent autonomy and the minimum controls each one needs before it touches a customer: https://lnkd.in/enwDF5an
